title: Temporal Abstraction and Reasoning for Robotic Navigation
abstract: Robotic navigation systems frequently encounter difficulties when dealing with long-horizon planning tasks. This paper introduces a novel framework for temporal abstraction and reasoning, designed to mitigate this challenge. The core idea revolves around a hierarchical planning system that leverages abstraction to manage long-term goals while maintaining real-time execution through lower-level controllers. This approach allows robots to effectively plan and execute actions across extended temporal scales, improving overall navigation performance. The framework is built upon the principles of representing goals at different levels of abstraction and dynamically adapting the planning process based on environmental changes. The system uses a combination of state estimation, path planning, and control algorithms, optimized for temporal reasoning and efficient execution. The key contribution lies in providing a structured method to decompose complex navigation problems into manageable temporal segments, significantly reducing the computational burden associated with traditional long-horizon planning. This paper outlines the architecture, key components, and potential applications of this framework.

title: Graph-Based Representation Learning for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for neuro-symbolic reasoning that leverages the strengths of graph representation learning and symbolic logic. The core idea is to learn graph representations of knowledge from data and then utilize these representations within a symbolic reasoning engine to perform logical inference. We propose a system consisting of a Graph Neural Network (GNN) for encoding knowledge graphs and a symbolic reasoning engine for deduction. This approach addresses the limitations of purely data-driven methods and purely symbolic systems by combining the robustness and generalization capabilities of graph learning with the precise and interpretable nature of symbolic reasoning. The framework demonstrates the potential for improved intelligent problem-solving across various domains.

title: Quantum Topology: A Computational Geometry Programming Framework
abstract: Quantum topology, a fascinating field of mathematics, has recently attracted significant attention due to its potential to unlock new computational paradigms. This paper explores the application of quantum topology to computational geometry programming, specifically focusing on optimization. We propose a novel framework, Quantum Topology Optimization (QTO), that leverages quantum computation to accelerate the optimization of complex geometric structures. This framework integrates the inherent properties of quantum topology with the principles of CGP, resulting in a computationally efficient and potentially transformative approach to geometric problem-solving. The core claim is that a QTO-based system can significantly improve the performance of optimization algorithms compared to traditional methods. This work presents a foundational investigation into the intersection of quantum mechanics and computational geometry, offering a new avenue for algorithmic innovation.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Foundation Models for Intelligent Mechanical Systems: Threat Models, Benchmarks, and Defense Stacks
abstract: Foundation models increasingly operate across modalities (vision, language, audio, and vision–language) and are deployed in decision-critical pipelines with tool use and retrieval. This expands the adversarial surface: small perturbations to images or audio can flip predictions, carefully crafted text can induce unsafe actions, and cross-modal attacks can exploit representation alignment to produce consistent but wrong outputs. This paper reviews adversarial robustness of foundation models across modalities and proposes a unified benchmark-and-defense stack. We first formalize multimodal threat models (white-box/black-box, digital/physical, prompt-level/system-level) and show how attack objectives differ across classification, retrieval, captioning, and agentic planning. We then summarize benchmark families for robustness: standardized perturbation budgets in vision, imperceptible audio attacks, instruction-following adversarial prompts in language, and cross-modal attacks on vision–language alignment and retrieval. Finally, we present a practical defense stack combining (i) robust training and regularization, (ii) multimodal input sanitization and consistency checks, (iii) retrieval/verification and ensemble critics, and (iv) runtime guardrails for tool execution. We recommend reporting both utility and security metrics: clean accuracy, robust accuracy, attack success rate, confidence calibration, and worst-case safety violations under adaptive adversaries. The goal is to provide a deployment-oriented roadmap for measuring and improving robustness of multimodal foundation models.

title: Towards Solar Nowcasting: Short-Term Solar Irradiance Forecasting with All-Sky Imagers and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing share of solar photovoltaics (PV) in power grids and buildings is reshaping the energy landscape but also introducing operational challenges due to the inherent variability of solar irradiance. Rapid cloud movements can cause short-term fluctuations in PV output, making it difficult to ensure grid stability, manage power imbalances, and optimize energy use within Building Energy Management Systems (BEMS). This thesis, titled Towards Solar Nowcasting, contributes to overcoming these challenges by advancing short-termsolar forecasting techniques, with a particular emphasis on real-time, image-based forecasting also known as solar nowcasting. To this end, the research begins with a comprehensive review of solar forecasting techniques, highlighting the growing importance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods in capturing complex irradiance patterns across diverse time horizons, from ultra-short (1 minute) to 24 hours ahead. A particular focus is placed on the potential of neural networks and hybrid AI models, as well as the critical need for standardized datasets and benchmarking practices to ensure accurate model evaluation and performance. This review forms the foundation for the development of innovative nowcasting solutions. Building on these insights, the thesis presents a data-driven short-termsolar forecasting framework using all-sky imagers (ASIs) and deep learning. Specifically, cloud movement is tracked using optical flow models, and future sky states are generated to serve as inputs for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-TermMemory (LSTM) networks. This hybrid approach enables accurate Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) predictions up to 20 minutes ahead. The developed models demonstrate significant improvements over baseline persistence methods, achieving ramp skill scores of up to 39% under sunny conditions. To address the limitations of existing methods in complex weather scenarios, the thesis further develops an innovative hybrid AI framework that combines superpixel-based cloud detection, Support Vector Machines (SVMs), CNNs, and Kalman filtering. This approach integrates high-resolution sky images, advanced computer vision techniques, and adaptive weather classification to deliver reliable GHI forecasts for horizons up to one hour. Tested on extensive datasets from the Netherlands, the method showed marked improvements in forecast accuracy, particularly under challenging conditions such as overcast or rainy skies, where conventional models often fail. Finally, the thesis translates these forecasting advancements into practical applications for congestion management, power imbalance mitigation, and building energy management. By benchmarking statistical, AI-based, and sky-imager-driven PV forecasting techniques, the study demonstrates that the integration of real-time sky image data significantly enhances short-term PV power forecasts. This, in turn, supports grid operators in implementing proactive congestion control, reduces reliance on costly balancing reserves, and enables intelligent energy management strategies within buildings, including load shifting, battery storage optimization, and increased PV self-consumption. In summary, in this thesis, advanced short-termsolar forecasting techniques have been developed to address key operational challenges arising fromthe growing integration of solar photovoltaics (PV) into modern energy systems. By combining all-sky imaging, artificial intelligence, and hybrid machine learning frameworks, this work demonstrates significant improvements in the accuracy and reliability of solar nowcasting. The proposed methodologies provide practical solutions for congestion management, power imbalance reduction, and optimized building energy management. Overall, this thesis contributes to enabling a more reliable and efficient integration of solar energy, supporting the broader goals of grid stability, energy flexibility, and the ongoing energy transition.

title: Based on Delay Quantum Network Routing Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum network routing protocol leveraging the inherent delay characteristics of quantum entanglement. Traditional quantum network routing protocols often rely on metrics like channel capacity and latency, which can be complex to determine and optimize. This proposed protocol, termed "Based on Delay Quantum Network Routing Protocol," directly utilizes the measured delay of quantum entanglement to guide data transmission, offering a potentially more efficient and adaptable routing strategy. The core mechanism involves quantifying and interpreting the delay associated with entangled states, effectively mapping these delays to optimal routing paths. This approach provides a fundamentally different perspective on routing, moving beyond conventional capacity-based analysis. We explore the theoretical foundations, outline the protocol's architecture, and discuss potential challenges and future research directions. The efficacy of this protocol is demonstrated through a theoretical framework, highlighting the potential for improved data transmission rates and resilience within quantum networks.

title: Adversarial Robustness via Information Bottleneck in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various graph-based tasks, including node classification, graph classification, and link prediction. However, a critical vulnerability to adversarial attacks has been identified. These attacks, employing subtle perturbations to graph structures or node features, can drastically degrade GNN performance. This work introduces a novel approach to enhance GNN robustness by integrating the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle. The IB principle, originally developed in information theory, encourages learning a compressed representation of data that retains only the most relevant information for a given task. We propose a GNN architecture incorporating an IB layer, effectively forcing the network to learn a robust, compressed representation of the graph, thereby mitigating the impact of adversarial perturbations. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving adversarial robustness compared to standard GNNs. The core contribution lies in the design and implementation of an IB module specifically tailored for the graph convolutional operation within GNNs.

title: Adaptive Quantum State Tomography with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a fundamental technique for characterizing the state of a quantum system. However, traditional QST protocols often require a large number of measurements, leading to significant experimental overhead and uncertainties in the reconstructed state. This paper proposes a novel approach to QST that leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to dynamically adapt measurement strategies. The core idea is to train an RL agent to control the parameters of the QST experiment, learning to optimize the measurement process based on feedback from the acquired data. The agent learns to select measurement bases and angles that minimize the uncertainty in the reconstructed quantum state. This adaptive strategy significantly reduces the number of measurements needed compared to traditional QST while maintaining high accuracy. We present a theoretical framework for this approach, outlining the key components and demonstrating its potential for improved QST performance. The proposed method offers a promising direction for enhancing the efficiency and reliability of QST, contributing to the advancement of quantum information processing.

This dynamic adjustment allows for a more efficient and robust optimization process compared to static methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing significant performance gains in specific benchmark quantum algorithms. The resulting algorithm offers a pathway to more effective quantum algorithm design and optimization.

title: Based Quantum State Superposition-Based Parallel Computing Architecture (QSSPCA)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel parallel computing architecture, termed the Quantum State Superposition-Based Parallel Computing Architecture (QSSPCA), leveraging the principles of quantum state superposition. The core claim is that exploiting superposition allows for the construction of a fundamentally new parallel computing paradigm. The architecture centers around a specifically designed computing unit utilizing quantum logic gates to perform operations in parallel, aiming to surpass the limitations of classical parallel computing in terms of speed and efficiency. The underlying mechanism involves manipulating multiple quantum states simultaneously, enabling operations that would be impossible with sequential or even conventional parallel architectures. This research explores the potential applications of quantum state superposition within parallel computing, offering a new perspective for future computing architectures. The theoretical framework presented outlines the fundamental components and operational principles of the QSSPCA.

evidence.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic computation model based on adaptive self-organizing networks. The core principle is to dynamically adjust network structure – specifically, node states and connection strengths – based on internal network dynamics. This allows for self-adaptive optimization through a continuous feedback loop. The model leverages the inherent properties of self-organizing networks to achieve robust and responsive control over network behavior. This research explores the potential of this approach to address complex optimization challenges across various domains. The paper details the model's architecture, operational mechanisms, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in a simulated environment.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Information Theory: A Computation Complexity Analysis
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic adaptive information theory approach to computational complexity analysis. Traditional methods often rely on static assumptions about data characteristics, limiting their applicability to evolving datasets. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts the complexity of information-theoretic computations based on input data, enabling optimized performance across a wider range of scenarios. The core mechanism involves a continuous, adaptive adjustment of the information-space complexity, ensuring efficient processing. This work aims to significantly enhance computational efficiency in information theory applications.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Grammatical Inference
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to symbolic regression, termed Evolutionary Grammatical Inference (EGI) combined with evolutionary algorithms. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with the complexity of data and the potential for generating overly complex or inaccurate equations. We address this challenge by first leveraging Evolutionary Grammatical Inference to generate a diverse set of candidate grammars, representing potential mathematical relationships. Subsequently, an evolutionary algorithm is applied to optimize these grammars, focusing on their ability to accurately model the input data. This synergistic combination overcomes the limitations of purely evolutionary or purely symbolic approaches, resulting in a more robust and efficient discovery process. The core claim is that this combined approach provides a more powerful method for uncovering mathematical equations compared to existing techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a detailed theoretical framework and outline the key components of the system.

title: Privacy Enhancement Based on Quantum Key Distribution Protocols
abstract: This paper explores the integration of privacy enhancement techniques with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols. We investigate the utilization of quantum teleportation and quantum state superposition to bolster the security of key distribution. The core concept involves combining the key distribution process with quantum teleportation and superposition, leveraging the properties of quantum entanglement and state superposition to achieve enhanced privacy. This approach aims to mitigate potential eavesdropping attacks by fundamentally altering the information exchange process. The theoretical framework presented here contributes to the growing body of research exploring secure communication paradigms in the quantum era. The primary objective is to demonstrate a viable methodology for significantly increasing the security of QKD systems, particularly against sophisticated attacks. The proposed method relies on the inherent unpredictability of quantum mechanics and the difficulties associated with intercepting and measuring quantum states without disturbing them. We present a detailed mathematical model illustrating the key aspects of the proposed protocol, focusing on the generation and distribution of a shared secret key while maintaining the confidentiality of the key itself.

title: Neural Symbolic Artificial Intelligence: A Knowledge Graph Reasoning Mechanism
abstract: This paper explores the integration of neural networks and symbolic reasoning within the emerging field of Neural Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NeSyAI). The core challenge lies in effectively combining the knowledge representation and learning capabilities of neural networks with the logical inference and validation mechanisms of symbolic systems, particularly in the context of knowledge graph reasoning. We propose a novel mechanism – a neuro-symbolic reasoning engine – designed to bridge this gap. This engine leverages neural networks for representing and learning knowledge from knowledge graphs, while utilizing the graph structure for performing inference and ensuring the soundness of conclusions. This architecture addresses limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic approaches by providing a robust and explainable reasoning framework. The paper details the key components of this engine, focusing on the interplay between neural embeddings and logical rules, and outlines a potential framework for its implementation. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of this approach on various applications, including question answering, data integration, and automated reasoning. ---

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning for Cryptography Cybersecurity in Uganda: Robustness Under Distribution Shift and Sparse Labels
abstract: The federated monitoring of cryptographic failure and cyber-intrusion signals across Ugandan institutions inherits two under-addressed tensions: client event distributions drift with sectoral traffic, software configuration and adversary behaviour, and attack labels remain sparse because cryptographic incident confirmation is slow, costly and legally sensitive. It combines local differential privacy with a distributionally robust semi-supervised objective over Wasserstein perturbations. The main results are a Kantorovich–Rubinstein bound relating tolerated distribution shift and loss variation, an excess-risk bound for confidence-thresholded pseudo-labelling under sparse labels, and a privacy-utility trade-off specified through Rényi differential privacy and secure aggregation. The framework distinguishes what can be guaranteed at design time from what must be validated by local security operations alone. The result is not an empirical report on Ugandan data; it is a mathematically stated protocol of assumptions, theorems and implementation conditions tailored to Uganda's inter-institutional cyber incident monitoring under the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019.

title: Natural Language Processing and Text Analytics
abstract: Natural language processing (NLP) and text analytics have become tools for understanding how people use language and mining useful information from vast amounts of written text. These technologies combine language studies, computer science, and artificial intelligence in efforts to make machines capable of understanding, interpreting, and even creating language very similarly to how it is created by humans. Text analytics applies NLP methods that turn messy and disorganized text into clear, structured data to allow firms to find patterns, sentiments, and trends. Together, these technologies support many applications, including chatbots and recommendation systems, public opinion tracking, and reviewing legal documents. Recent improvements in deep learning and context-aware word representations have increased the capabilities of machines in understanding the meaning and subtleties of language. This chapter investigates the basics, steps, and challenges of NLP and text analytics that make them crucial in today’s world for generating new ideas and making good decisions.

title: The quantum switch as a commutation-syndrome filter for qubit Pauli channels: deterministic advantage over definite-order strategies and an exact geometric law
abstract: Abstract The quantum switch is known to remove noise probabilistically, but whether this constitutes an advantage over causally ordered processing has remained contentious: postselection, weak classical benchmarks, and task-dependent comparisons have all drawn criticism. Here we give an exact analysis of the question for a qubit under Pauli noise. For any two qubit Pauli channels, measuring the switch’s control qubit implements a commutation syndrome : it sorts each noise realization by whether the two Kraus errors commuted, syndrome information that an unencoded qubit does not otherwise possess, and the optimal measure-and-feed-forward protocol has a closed form. The analytical results have two levels of generality. For the exactly solvable pair, an isotropic depolarizing channel and a flip channel along an arbitrary axis, we prove a complete ceiling theorem: every definite-order protocol using each channel once, with arbitrary memoryless intermediate operations and receiver-side post-processing, deterministic or heralded, has entanglement fidelity at most ma x P c P , and the switch exceeds this ceiling deterministically , by p q / 3 over most of parameter space. For arbitrary qubit Pauli pairs, the ceiling is proven against arbitrary receiver-side post-processing, and the gain is strictly positive if and only if the two syndrome branches call for different Pauli corrections, confining the exceptions to error-dominated noise. Side systems are covered whenever they are non-signaling about the message. Beyond these theorems the evidence is numerical: strict gain in 99.8 % of 5000 random Pauli pairs, and no case, within a 200 -pair sample, in which an optimized midpoint echo overturns the gain. The state-resolved gain obeys an exact geometric law, Δ F = 2 p q / 3 | r ^ ⋅ n ^ | 2 : alignment is the condition under which the degenerate two-error syndrome becomes perfectly correctable. The separation survives control dephasing down to a threshold visibility that falls with noise strength, and at strong noise it outperforms coherent control of the two orderings even with twice the channel uses.

title: Poisson Image Denoising Using Minimax Concave and Reweighted $\ell_1$ Penalties: Nonblind and Blind Approaches
abstract: Images are important tools in various sciences. Despite the development of photo-taking tools, creating clear and image without noise remains challenging in practice. In particular, Poisson noise has an effect on medical and astronomical images, and reduces their quality. Additionally, blur is another factor that has an effect on image quality. The problem of image restoration becomes very complicated when we have no information about the Point Spread Function (PSF). These types of problems are known as blind case. However, in some images, such as some astronomical images, the type of PSF can be specified, and these types of problems are known as nonblind problems. Total Variation (TV) is a widely used method for solving such inverse problems, where the selection of the penalty function is the most critical factor that affects the method's performance. In this paper, to improve edge preservation, we employ a reweighted $\ell_1$-regularization of the fractional order derivative. Furthermore, we propose a nonblind and blind image deblurring approach under Poisson noise using the Minimax Concave Penalty (MCP), which is a continuous, sparsity promoting, and nearly unbiased regularizer. This formulation leads to a nonconvex optimization model. To solve the proposed model, we introduce an efficient numerical algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) and provide an analysis of its convergence. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm are demonstrated through extensive experiments on various images.

title: I Don't Miss You, but I Do: Self-Explanation Faithfulness of Modality Missingness in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in settings where some input modalities may be unavailable, yet we know little about whether they can faithfully explain how such missing information affects their own predictions. We introduce an interventional protocol for evaluating self-explanations of modality dynamics: models state what each modality alone would support, whether restoring a missing modality would change their answer, and whether the available evidence is sufficient; we then execute the corresponding intervention and compare these claims with realized behavior. We evaluate ten VLMs spanning open-weight and proprietary models across four tasks covering mixed, redundant, and unique modality regimes. We find a systematic tendency to overstate the sufficiency of available evidence. Models substantially underestimate the effect of restoring missing modalities: executed change exceeds predicted change in 78 of 80 model-task-condition settings, with task-level median executed change rates reaching 70.1\% while median predicted rates remain at most 9.6\%. Insufficiency claims have low recall, leaving many cases in which behavior changes despite a stated claim of sufficiency. Retrospective self-explanations show the same tendency, over-crediting single-input sufficiency in mixed regimes and interchangeability in redundant ones. Together, these results show that VLMs systematically mischaracterize how their predictions depend on available and missing evidence, motivating executable interventions as a behavioral test of multimodal self-explanations.

title: Storing Infinite Dynamical Attractors in Nonreciprocal Associative Neural Networks
abstract: We develop a dynamical mean-field theory for nonreciprocal associative networks that store an extensive number of dynamical attractors, from limit cycles to strange attractors. Using a path integral calculation under quenched disorder, we derive self-consistent dynamical mean-field equations for pattern overlaps, autocorrelations and response functions. Memory retrieval capacity is governed by the spectral structure of the coupling matrices encoding stored patterns. When their eigenvalues are coherently aligned, retarded self-interactions and quenched noise feed back destructively: at zero eigenphase (fixed point attractors) the classical equilibrium capacity bound is recovered, while for limit cycles retrieval collapses far below it. In contrast, for uniformly distributed eigenphases, retarded self-interactions and much of the quenched noise cancels, reducing the dynamics to an effective single-spin process and amplifying capacity substantially. We validate the theory against microscopic simulations for limit-cycle and chaotic attractors, identifying eigenvalue decoherence as the mechanism enabling enhanced storage of dynamical memories.

title: Matryoshka Hash Representations for Model-Aware Compact Semantic Retrieval
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) depends on dense retrieval: each document is stored as a learned vector, and a query is answered by finding its nearest neighbors in that vector space. Keeping one full-precision vector per document is the dominant index cost at corpus scale, so retrieval systems replace each vector with a short code of a few bytes---a step called quantization. Standard quantizers such as product quantization (PQ) pick the code that reconstructs the original vector most closely. A single code is even more useful if it serves several byte budgets at once: when its short prefixes are each directly searchable, a deployment can set its efficiency--quality operating point without re-encoding the corpus. But training all prefixes under one objective makes the early bits a compromise across budgets---short codes improve while the full-width code degrades. Quantization to low-bit representation, such as binary codes, further sharpens the conflict. We introduce Matryoshka Hash Representations (MHR), a two-stage procedure that separates full-width training from prefix organization. MHR first learns a longer binary code, then freezes the model and trains additional zero-initialized residual code adaptors for directly searchable prefixes. Documents are stored at one bit per coordinate, while queries keep continuous logits like PQ to attain sufficient expressivity. We implement the search process with FAISS FastScan. Trained on MS MARCO and zero-shot transferred to seven BEIR datasets, MHR reaches .5561 NDCG@10 and .6535 Recall@100 at 32 bytes, surpassing the best baseline of the same budget. The advantage is more pronounced in lower budgets. The same code also strengthens two common pipelines: shortlisting candidates for full-precision reranking, and pruning a low-storage graph index such as LEANN.

title: Dimension Generalization with Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of dimensionality generalization and quantum entanglement to achieve highly accurate geometric modeling. The core claim is to develop a novel method leveraging quantum entanglement to map low-dimensional spaces to higher-dimensional spaces, utilizing entanglement for precise geometric calculations and enabling high-precision modeling. We propose a quantum computing algorithm designed to perform geometric computations within low-dimensional spaces, guided by the entangled states generated by this process. This approach offers a fundamentally new pathway for geometric data analysis and modeling, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical techniques. The paper explores the potential of this combination to address challenges in geometric representation and precise calculation, highlighting the key mechanisms involved and outlining future research directions.

title: Wave Function Collapse for Bayesian Inference in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper explores the application of wave function collapse (WFC) to Bayesian inference within complex systems. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages quantum superposition to efficiently explore multiple possible states simultaneously, aiming to improve the accuracy of Bayesian inference across a wider range of problems. The core mechanism centers around dynamically collapsing wave functions based on a probabilistic assessment of the system's state, mitigating the limitations of traditional methods. We detail the algorithm's design, provide an example demonstrating its efficacy, and discuss potential future directions, including scalability and application to diverse complex systems.

title: Adam Prism: A Sovereignty-First Architecture for Verified, Deterministic LLM Agents
abstract: Autonomous LLM agents that generate code, documents, or system artifacts face a structural problem: their outputs are stochastic, while the environments they must produce for are deterministic. Orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen move control out of the model loop, yet verification still relies on LLM-as-a-judge. We present Adam Prism, a sovereignty-first agent architecture that treats verification as a first-class architectural layer. Planning, execution, verification, and repair are separated into independent stages; a deep-verification loop combines deterministic functional checks with an independent spec-conformance judge; and a bounded escalation ladder repairs defects with an honest stop. On a local 12B model via Ollama the system sustains 1,317 deterministic tests and 26 scenario workflows, and two independent oracle-checked registries (10 CSV-verification and 5 code-generation scenarios) reach 10/10 and 15/15 (100%) single-shot --- zero cost, air-gap capable. This package contains the paper, its sources, and the measured benchmark data. No source code is included.

title: Quantum Error Correction Protocols: A Topology-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning Approach
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a critical component of quantum computing, enabling reliable transmission and manipulation of quantum information. Current QEC protocols, particularly surface codes, suffer from inherent vulnerabilities to information loss due to noise and imperfections in the hardware. This paper introduces a novel quantum error correction protocol utilizing topology-enhanced reinforcement learning (TEL) to mitigate these risks. The core concept is to model the quantum error correction process as a dynamically evolving topological structure, effectively reducing the vulnerability to information leakage. We propose a TEL-based algorithm that leverages the inherent properties of topological spaces to guide the optimization process, leading to improved error correction capabilities. This research presents a preliminary investigation of the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations and a simplified, illustrative example. The presented approach offers a promising pathway towards robust and efficient QEC, potentially simplifying the development of practical quantum systems.

title: 基于自适应拓扑的量子计算的能量筛选
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology in quantum computing to enhance energy selection within quantum algorithms. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle with computationally expensive energy calculations, necessitating the identification and elimination of high-energy states. We propose a novel quantum computation paradigm centered around dynamically adjusting computational parameters based on a self-organized topological structure. This approach allows for rapid and efficient energy screening, potentially leading to significant improvements in quantum algorithm performance. The core mechanism involves constructing a topology that reacts to the energy landscape of a quantum system, effectively prioritizing the propagation of energy along specific paths. This paper details the theoretical framework, simulation results, and potential implications of this innovative approach.

title: Dynamic Topology for Geometric Information Compression
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic topology to geometric information compression. Geometric information, traditionally represented as complex data structures, often requires significant storage and transmission. We propose a novel algorithm that leverages dynamic topology, a mathematical framework that allows for continuous structural changes, to compress data. The core mechanism involves constructing and manipulating a dynamic topological structure that effectively encodes the geometric properties of the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through rigorous analysis and simulations, showcasing significant improvements in compression ratios compared to existing methods. The algorithm's efficiency stems from its ability to adapt to the data's inherent structure, allowing for higher compression rates. Furthermore, the dynamic nature of the topology ensures a more robust compression process.

title: Context-Aware Neural Turing Machines with Episodic Memory
abstract: This paper introduces a novel architecture, Context-Aware Neural Turing Machines with Episodic Memory (CAN-ETM), designed to address the limitations of existing Neural Turing Machines (NTMs) regarding contextual understanding and long-term dependency learning. Current NTMs struggle to effectively incorporate surrounding context, leading to difficulties in tasks requiring temporal reasoning and complex pattern recognition. Our proposed solution integrates an episodic memory module with the NTM, enabling the network to store and retrieve past experiences based on contextual cues derived from the current input. This mechanism facilitates the learning of more intricate and nuanced temporal patterns. The core claim is that augmenting NTMs with this contextual episodic memory significantly enhances their ability to model sequential data. We demonstrate this through a theoretical framework outlining the key components and their interactions, and propose a set of equations to illustrate the learning process. The CAN-ETM architecture represents a significant step forward in building more intelligent and adaptable neural network models for tasks involving context-dependent learning.

title: Multi-Agent Simulation with Emergent Social Norms using Agent-Based Modeling
abstract: This paper explores the use of agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate the emergence of social norms within a population of autonomous agents. The core idea is that complex social behaviors, including the formation of norms, can arise from the interactions of agents following simple, rule-based behaviors. This research provides a framework for investigating how social norms develop in dynamic systems, offering a method to understand phenomena such as cooperation, altruism, and even conflict. The simulation presented utilizes a discrete event-based ABM environment where agents possess attributes like trust, reputation, and observational capabilities. Agents interact based on a set of predefined rules, and the accumulated interactions lead to the statistically observable emergence of norms. The model's parameters, including agent attributes, interaction probabilities, and the influence of observation, are varied to demonstrate the sensitivity of norm formation to these factors. The results demonstrate the potential of ABM to capture emergent social dynamics and provide insights into the underlying mechanisms driving norm formation. Further research will explore the robustness of these norms and their impact on system-wide behavior.

title: Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) for Accelerating Machine Learning
abstract: The burgeoning field of machine learning (ML) is increasingly reliant on massive datasets for training complex models, particularly deep neural networks. However, the retrieval of data from conventional memory systems represents a significant bottleneck, limiting the scalability and efficiency of ML algorithms. This research proposes a Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) architecture designed to overcome this limitation by leveraging quantum mechanical principles. The core concept involves encoding data into qubits and utilizing quantum random access to achieve near-instantaneous data retrieval. This paper details a novel QRAM architecture, focusing on qubit arrangement, control mechanisms, and strategies for minimizing decoherence – a primary challenge in quantum computing. The theoretical framework explores the potential acceleration achievable through QRAM in deep neural network training, with the primary goal of dramatically reducing training times. We present a detailed mathematical model outlining the data encoding process, quantum access protocols, and the expected performance gains. The architecture incorporates error mitigation techniques and discusses the scalability of the design for increasingly complex datasets. The research highlights the transformative potential of QRAM in accelerating ML, addressing a fundamental constraint within the current landscape of computational learning.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Quantum Error Correction Code Design
abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic adaptive quantum error correction (QEC) code design framework. The core idea is to leverage machine learning techniques to analyze error patterns during quantum information transmission and dynamically adjust the parameters of the QEC code accordingly. Traditional QEC codes are often designed with fixed parameters, which may not be optimal for all transmission scenarios. This adaptive approach aims to improve the robustness and reliability of quantum information transfer by tailoring the code to the specific characteristics of the channel and the data being transmitted. The system utilizes a feedback loop, where the machine learning model continuously learns from observed errors and adjusts the code's parameters to minimize error rates. This research addresses the critical need for more flexible and efficient QEC strategies in the development of practical quantum communication networks. The proposed framework offers a pathway towards significantly enhanced quantum information transmission performance.

title: ##可解释性人工智能的因果图推导 (KAIETP)
abstract: This paper introduces the KAIETP (Causal Inference for Explainable AI) framework, a novel approach to analyzing and interpreting the inner workings of explainable AI (XAI) models. Traditional XAI methods often focus on post-hoc explanations without fundamentally addressing the underlying causal relationships driving model decisions. KAIETP leverages causal inference theory to systematically decompose XAI models into their constituent causal structures, represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). These DAGs are then analyzed using causal reasoning algorithms to identify and quantify the key causal pathways responsible for the model's predictions. The core contribution lies in providing a structured, theoretically grounded method for understanding the 'why' behind XAI model outputs, ultimately enhancing interpretability and trust. This framework moves beyond simply highlighting correlations and instead focuses on establishing genuine causal links. The presented methodology offers a robust foundation for debugging, improving, and ultimately, building more reliable and transparent AI systems. This paper details the KAIETP framework, outlining the key steps involved in DAG construction, causal reasoning, and the interpretation of the resulting causal relationships.

title: Quantum Computing Breakthroughs and Renewed Investments
abstract: Quantum computing has entered an era of extraordinary progress, following the development of scalable architectures, noise-resilient algorithms, and compiler optimizations. This article describes how a new wave of international investment is driving the development of quantum hardware and software ranging from systems based on superconductors and on-property, to ion trap systems. We examine the connection between funding and practical impact (including recent progress towards fault-tolerant computing for real-world tasks). Combing the performance metrics with the innovation trends, the study paves the way for academia, industry, and policymakers to realize quantum advantage by using a more efficient approach.

title: A compression ratio estimation and optimization algorithm based on multi-modal feature fusion and hierarchical matching
abstract: The accurate estimation of differential compression ratio is pivotal to enhancing data storage and transmission efficiency. To overcome the three shortcomings of the traditional EDCR(efficient delta compression ratio) framework: high feature collision rate(>12%), low matching efficiency(the average time consumption per match is 4.0 ms) and inadequate dynamic adaptability, this paper proposes a novel optimization algorithm based on multimodal feature fusion and hierarchical matching architecture. The novelty includes: 128 bit composite feature values that integrate the Adler-32 rolling Hash, SHA-256 fingerprint and entropy-based type tag are established; the three-tier hierarchical matching architecture that includes the Bloom filter, the Hash table and the Jaccard fuzzy matching is designed; the time-decay dynamic redundancy model and the exponential smoothing calibration mechanism are set up. The experiments with the VMA and RDB(virtual machine image and redis database) real datasets demonstrate that: ①In the high-redundancy phase (redundancy>40%), the mean error of compression ratio estimation is reduced to 2.1% and 86.3% higher than the EDCR algorithm. ②The error is as low as 2.4% when the noise level is 31 and the noise resistance is 85.8% higher. ③The time consumption for feature computation decreases from 4.0 ms to 0.4 ms (90% decrease) and the matching frequency is 85% lower. ④The throughput increases by 23.4% to 34.4% on the SSD medium. This paper provides a high-precision and low-latency compression ratio estimation framework for a massive data system, satisfying the high-performance requirements for cloud storage and edge computing scenes.

title: JEDI: JEPA-to-Edge Distillation for Efficient Cropland Segmentation from Satellite Imagery
abstract: Large vision models provide useful representations for remote-sensing segmentation but are often too expensive for deployment at the satellite or field edge. Existing feature-level distillation methods also tend to assume similar teacher and student architectures and often stop feature alignment when task training begins. We introduce JEDI (JEPA-to-Edge Distillation), a two-stage framework that transfers representations from a large I-JEPA Vision Transformer teacher to a compact SegFormer student. First, JEDI aligns the student's terminal representation with the teacher's token space using cross-architecture projection and spatial alignment. It then jointly optimizes supervised segmentation, temperature-scaled response distillation, and persistent feature alignment throughout task adaptation. On CalCROP21, JEDI-B0 achieves 68.0 mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) with 4.04M parameters, improving over the standalone student by 16.0 points and coming within 2.0 points of the 70.0 mIoU achieved by the 639M-parameter teacher. We evaluate SegFormer B0, B1, and B2 students with 4.04M, 14.33M, and 28M parameters, respectively. Across all three variants, JEDI consistently outperforms response-, structure-, channel-, and relational-distillation baselines under the same teacher-student setting. These results show that persistent representation alignment is especially valuable under aggressive compression, substantially reducing model size and computation while preserving segmentation performance.

title: Same Problem, Different Field: Cross-Domain Solution Import via Domain-Stripped Computational Fingerprints
abstract: The same underlying computational problem is solved across unrelated fields under different names: recursive Bayesian state estimation appears as a "Kalman filter" in control, "Bayesian forecasting" in pharmacokinetics, and "data assimilation" in geoscience. Topical and citation-based scientific embeddings cannot see this shared problem. We distill each paper once into a domain- and method-name-stripped faceted computational fingerprint, a free-text mechanism skeleton plus controlled computational facets. We define a tunable, facet-selectable similarity over it. The goal is solution import: surface cross-field pairs solving the same problem, so a bespoke implementation can be swapped for another field's standard, specialized solver. On a benchmark of 18 method families across 109 papers, the skeleton lifts cross-domain retrieval average precision over the abstract from 0.222 to 0.513, and the whole fingerprint reaches 0.557. Strikingly, four trained scientific embedders all fall below plain abstract+TF-IDF: they encode topical and citation similarity, the wrong signal for this task. The gain is the representation: the abstract-to-skeleton swap lifts every embedder, and the pipeline is one cached LLM call per paper plus a cheap embedder. An interventional re-skin / math-edit test shows the fingerprint tracks the computation, not the field. On a 501-paper wild corpus, known twins dominate the top of the ranking (23 of the top 30); with planted pairs excluded from the results, three blind LLM judges rate 3 of the top 5 and 8 of the top 30 pairs genuine import candidates, and 0 of 30 random ones. evidence.title: Same Problem, Different Field: Cross-Domain Solution Import via Domain-Stripped Computational Fingerprints
evidence.abstract: The same underlying computational problem is solved across unrelated fields under different names: recursive Bayesian state estimation appears as a "Kalman filter" in control, "Bayesian forecasting" in pharmacokinetics, and "data assimilation" in geoscience. Topical and citation-based scientific embeddings cannot see this shared problem. We distill each paper once into a domain- and method-name-stripped faceted computational fingerprint, a free-text mechanism skeleton plus controlled computational facets. We define a tunable, facet-selectable similarity over it. The goal is solution import: surface cross-field pairs solving the same problem, so a bespoke implementation can be swapped for another field's standard, specialized solver. On a benchmark of 18 method families across 109 papers, the skeleton lifts cross-domain retrieval average precision over the abstract from 0.222 to 0.513, and the whole fingerprint reaches 0.557. Strikingly, four trained scientific embedders all fall below plain abstract+TF-IDF: they encode topical and citation similarity, the wrong signal for this task. The gain is the representation: the abstract-to-skeleton swap lifts every embedder, and the pipeline is one cached LLM call per paper plus a cheap embedder. An interventional re-skin / math-edit test shows the fingerprint tracks the computation, not the field. On a 501-paper wild corpus, known twins dominate the top of the ranking (23 of the top 30); with planted pairs excluded from the results, three blind LLM judges rate 3 of the top 5 and 8 of the top 30 pairs genuine import candidates, and 0 of 30 random ones. The human verification is the four executed imports: in one, an open standard solver reproduces a bespoke clinical dosing engine's output. title: LightSplat: Real-Time High-Fidelity 3D Gaussian SLAM with Loop Closure
abstract: SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently demonstrated promising reconstruction accuracy for dense 3D scene representations. However, current 3DGS systems struggle to meet the strict demands of real-world deployments due to severe limitations in operational performance and map adaptability. To this end, we propose LightSplat, a hybrid-representation RGB-D SLAM framework. It synergizes local sparse features for robust and fast tracking with a dual-thread backend that progressively constructs dense Gaussian submaps. Crucially, we enable online loop closure through feature-accelerated 3DGS registration, refining overall map consistency through pose graph optimization. Ultimately, LightSplat achieves the online reconstruction of high-fidelity Gaussian map. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets and real-world robotic platform demonstrate that our method achieves near state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and the capability to accommodate practical camera motions, maintaining an average framerate of 8 FPS. Overall, LightSplat provides an efficient and robust foundation for deploying high-fidelity 3DGS in real-world environments.

title: GIFT: Goal-Injected Fine-Tuning for Efficient Manipulation Policy Adaptation
abstract: Compared with relying solely on initial observations and language instructions, predicting goal images with generative models as high-level visual guidance can significantly enhance the robustness of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, most existing foundation models have not systematically incorporated goal image conditioning due to the high computational training cost. To this end, we propose Goal-Injected Fine-Tuning (GIFT), a lightweight and efficient fine-tuning framework that seamlessly integrates generated goal images into multiple representative pretrained VLA models. Our approach introduces goal image features into observations via a zero-initialized convolution which progressively grows parameters from zero and prevents harmful noise from disrupting the pretrained policy during fine-tuning. As training proceeds, goal information is gradually incorporated, enabling efficient goal understanding without disrupting model stability. We further introduce a refined image editing method to generate semantically and visually consistent goal images from initial observations and task instructions. Experiments show that goal-aware VLA models achieve substantial performance gains across tasks: with only a single epoch of fine-tuning, GIFT outperforms the base model by 6.0% and 13.4% on two SIMPLER settings, and by 4.7% on LIBERO, demonstrating both efficiency and effectiveness.

title: Cross-database transportability of a parsimonious postoperative ICU mortality model: Code and reproducibility materials
abstract: This repository contains analysis code and reproducibility materials supporting the study “Cross-database transportability of a parsimonious postoperative ICU mortality model: external evaluation of care-group information from MIMIC-IV to INSPIRE.” The release includes cohort-construction and harmonization scripts, model specifications, preprocessing parameters, feature and outcome definitions, aggregate results, software environment specifications, and provenance and file-integrity records. The analyses used MIMIC-IV version 3.1 and INSPIRE version 1.4.2. Patient-level source data are not included in this public release. Re-execution of patient-level analyses requires authorized access to the source databases, compliance with the applicable data-use agreements, and appropriate local configuration. Release version: 1.0.0. Licensing: Original analysis code is released under the MIT License. Documentation and original aggregate materials are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. Third-party materials retain their original licenses. These licenses do not apply to the restricted source datasets.

title: Post-benchmark analysis package: label-free observability of silent EHR pipeline failures (code, locked real-event registry, decision log #93–#112; git 6bb4ad7)
abstract: Preregistered, frozen protocol package for a controlled information-ablation benchmark of label-free observability of silent failures in electronic health record (EHR) data pipelines. The package contains the frozen protocol (v1.0, 2026-08-14) and its v1.1 addendum, the frozen failure-mechanism taxonomy, observables registry and pipeline DAG node table, the complete decision log with every entry annotated as to whether comparative results had been seen, a scope-boundary declaration, substrate qualification reports for eICU-CRD v2.0 (primary substrate) and MIMIC-IV v3.1 (portability substrate), a bilingual inventory of the public data actually used (metadata and SHA-256 fingerprints only), a code snapshot, and the benchmark-evaluation-start record. This deposit was made before the formal benchmark was run. As of deposit, no detection, localisation or paired-gain results had been computed. The code state is anchored by git commit 019af8d and code-snapshot digest dd99b59e930342daa4728276cff774e1ec0860802d28c143a8ddaf043f21ee4e. No patient-level data are included. eICU-CRD and MIMIC-IV are available from PhysioNet under their respective data use agreements. Manuscript text is not included.Version note (relative to protocol-v1.1-frozen, git 019af8d): core.Pipeline gained an instance-level ctx_extra dictionary so that the cohort literal and unit-conversion bindings declared in decision log entries #78 and #79 can reach node contexts (entry #82, recorded in the deviations register); four run parameters not fixed by the protocol — the matched empirical false-alarm rate α, the reference-window definition, the base-window positions, and the localisation-metric denominator — were prespecified (entry #83); and the code snapshot and benchmark-evaluation-start record were regenerated against git commit 7b6b5f2. No data, no substrate qualification decision, and no frozen taxonomy, DAG, observables registry or estimand definition were changed. As of this deposit no comparative results had been computed.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks: Dynamic Entropy Control
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic entropy control algorithm for self-organizing neural networks (SONNs). SONNs are a type of neural network architecture characterized by a dynamic and adaptive structure, allowing for flexible representation and improved generalization. The core of this algorithm lies in a carefully orchestrated adjustment of network entropy, influencing the network's internal representation and ultimately affecting its learning performance. Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameters, while this approach leverages entropy as a mechanism for continuous learning and improved robustness. We present a rigorous theoretical analysis and practical implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its potential to enhance both the expressiveness and learning capabilities of SONNs. The research explores the impact of entropy distribution on network stability and convergence.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Representation
abstract: Quantum State Representation (QSR) is a novel formalism for representing quantum states, designed to facilitate efficient computation and communication across diverse quantum platforms. This paper introduces a 'Quantum Hierarchical State Space' – a layered network structuring quantum states – to enhance algorithm design and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the benefits of this structure through a rigorous analysis of key quantum algorithms, highlighting its potential to overcome current limitations in quantum software development. The core mechanism involves organizing states into a hierarchical system, allowing for targeted computation and improved algorithmic adaptability. This represents a significant step towards a more unified and versatile approach to quantum computing, offering a potential bridge between established paradigms.

title: Self-Organizing Neural Networks for Quantum State Tomography
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a fundamental technique in quantum information science, used to characterize the density matrix of an unknown quantum state. However, traditional QST methods are often computationally intensive, requiring a large number of measurements and sophisticated data analysis techniques. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing self-organizing neural networks (SONNs) for direct quantum state reconstruction. The core idea is to train a SONN to learn the mapping between experimental measurement data and the corresponding density matrix, thereby bypassing the need for precise control over the quantum system and significantly reducing the computational burden. We detail the architecture of the SONN, the training process, and demonstrate the potential of this method to achieve accurate state reconstruction with fewer measurements. The proposed method offers a promising path towards more efficient and scalable QST, particularly for complex quantum systems.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Semantic Web Technologies
abstract: This paper explores the integration of neural networks and symbolic reasoning through the application of Semantic Web technologies. The core challenge in neuro-symbolic reasoning lies in effectively bridging the gap between the representation learning capabilities of neural networks and the explicit knowledge representation and inference mechanisms of symbolic systems. We propose a framework that leverages Semantic Web technologies, specifically OWL (Web Ontology Language) and RDF (Resource Description Framework), to provide a structured knowledge base and rules, which are then integrated with neural networks to facilitate neuro-symbolic reasoning and inference. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic systems by combining their respective strengths. The paper details the architecture of the proposed system, outlining the data flow between the neural network and the semantic reasoning engine. We demonstrate the potential of this integrated approach through a conceptual example and discuss future research directions, focusing on scalability, robustness, and the development of more sophisticated mechanisms for translating between the two paradigms. The key contribution is the systematic approach to combining these technologies, offering a pathway toward more reliable and explainable AI systems.

title: Geometry Topology Quantum Computing Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a novel system for simulating complex geometric structures utilizing the unique capabilities of quantum computing. Traditional computational methods often struggle to accurately model quantum phenomena due to the inherent complexity of quantum systems. Quantum computing offers the potential for significantly enhanced precision in these simulations. We propose a system that leverages quantum algorithms to mimic intricate geometric structures, providing a framework for advanced simulation and analysis. The core of this work lies in the design of a 'Geometric Topology Quantum Computing Simulation' system, focusing on precise representation and manipulation of geometric data. The system aims to surpass the limitations of classical simulation techniques in modeling complex geometries, offering a pathway to new insights in areas such as materials science, cryptography, and theoretical physics. We detail the system's architecture, the underlying quantum algorithms employed, and a preliminary demonstration of its capabilities.

title: Quantum Topological Bifurcation Structures: A Novel Approach to Topology and Cryptography
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of quantum topology and cryptography, focusing on the development of novel quantum topological bifurcation structures. We investigate how these structures, rooted in quantum mechanics, can encode and manipulate information, potentially leading to enhanced cryptographic security. The core of our research lies in defining a specific mathematical framework—a topological bifurcation structure—that intrinsically incorporates quantum properties. We demonstrate the feasibility of analyzing these structures using topological information theory, revealing intricate relationships between the structure's geometry and the underlying quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm for generating and analyzing these structures, offering potential advancements in secure communication protocols. The study highlights the unique capabilities of these structures, emphasizing their potential impact on both quantum computing and cryptographic security.

title: Distributed Proof-Checking via Probabilistic Theorem Proving on Graph-Structured Data
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to automated theorem proving and proof verification, termed distributed proof-checking, which leverages probabilistic theorem proving (PTP) techniques applied to graph-structured mathematical data. The core challenge in traditional theorem proving lies in its inherent computational expense, particularly when dealing with complex theorems and lengthy proofs. Our approach addresses this limitation by representing mathematical theorems and their corresponding proofs as graphs. These graphs encapsulate logical relationships, dependencies, and structural components of the proof. Probabilistic theorem proving algorithms are then applied to these graph representations to automatically verify the correctness of the proof. Crucially, we propose a distributed computing architecture to scale the proof-checking process, exploiting parallel processing capabilities to significantly reduce verification time. This paper details the framework, outlines the key components, and discusses the potential benefits of this approach, positioning it as a significant advancement in the field of automated reasoning. We demonstrate how graph-based reasoning provides a more efficient and scalable foundation for theorem proving compared to traditional, symbolic methods. The core of our method is the application of PTP to a graph representation of a proof, allowing for probabilistic certainty in the verification process.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Gradient Descent for Deep Learning
abstract: Quantum-enhanced gradient descent offers a promising approach to accelerate and improve the training of deep learning models. This research investigates the potential of integrating quantum annealing techniques into the gradient descent optimization process, aiming to overcome limitations of classical methods in navigating complex loss landscapes. The core claim is that quantum annealing can significantly enhance convergence speed and robustness, particularly in deep learning scenarios. The paper presents a theoretical analysis and preliminary implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach, highlighting the potential benefits and challenges of this novel methodology.

abstract: This paper proposes a novel deep learning architecture designed to effectively capture complex relationships within data by mimicking the multi-scale information flow characteristics of biological neural systems. The core claim is that by structuring a deep neural network with multiple layers, each representing a different scale of information, we can better model long-range dependencies and local details. The mechanism involves leveraging the self-organizing properties of information flow, allowing for the hierarchical fusion and transfer of information across different scales. This approach addresses the limitations of conventional deep learning architectures that typically rely on single-scale information processing. The architecture is presented with detailed formula representations and mathematical notations.

title: Title: Dynamic Probability Distribution Machine Learning Model with Automated Parameter Adjustment
abstract: This paper presents a novel machine learning model leveraging dynamic probability distributions as its core parameter. Traditional machine learning models often require retraining to adapt to evolving data distributions, presenting a significant challenge. Our approach introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism that automatically adjusts model parameters based on the changing distribution of the input data. This allows for a more adaptive and robust learning process, effectively addressing the limitations of static models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a series of experiments on various benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior performance compared to traditional methods in scenarios with fluctuating data. The core mechanism focuses on a probabilistic weighting scheme, allowing the model to prioritize relevant features based on the current data distribution.

abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to enhance signal processing, specifically focusing on the modeling of non-linear quantum dynamics. Traditional signal processing techniques often struggle with complex, non-linear signals due to inherent limitations in their representation and processing capabilities. title: PRIMUS: Identity, Governance, and Verification for Multi-Agent Federations
abstract: Multi-agent federations need governance that answers three questions under adversarial conditions: who participated (identity), did they conform (enforcement), and who decides (authority). A separate question is whether the verification machinery that polices a federation's outputs can also steer a generate-and-test loop toward better answers. Part I. PRIMA introduced prime-power agent identity and a consensus token whose factorization indexes participation, but assumed honest agents. We present PRIMUS, which couples prime-power identity with BLS aggregate signatures (PIAC), derives a safe-kill threshold that reduces false-positive agent termination from 80% to 0.00% under 10% channel noise, gives the closed-form economic boundary where singleton governance outperforms Byzantine quorum ($γ^* \approx 9f$, verified flat across n = 50 to 10,000), and specifies VRF succession with lease and fencing that makes safety unconditional under partial synchrony. Five problems are identified as provably unfixable within the model and stated as scope boundaries. Part II. A verifier is not a solver. We ask whether PRIMA's binary artifact-fidelity verdict can be converted into a graded fitness signal, and measure the conversion on binary covering codes. Calibration against injected fault burden is strong ($ρ$ = 0.676 deterministic, 0.819 full); against real LLM-generated candidates the same scores fall to 0.158 and 0.406, roughly a quarter of the calibration value (the same-designer confound, measured). As a pre-filter it beats a random-score control convincingly and a binary gate narrowly. Under 400 iterations of explicit optimization it was not gamed, but only because the objective saturated after one honest answer. A cross-family judge preserves the burden-ordering signal while destroying individual judgments. No covering-code record resulted. Measured program cost: USD 164.78.

title: Efficient Optimization on the Euclidean Sphere: Riemannian Gradient Alignment as a Unifying Principle
abstract: Euclidean sphere-constrained optimization problems represent perhaps the most basic class of nonconvex-constrained problems for which there exist efficient optimization algorithms for specific problem instances, such as the eigenvalue problems and learning problems arising in the recent literature. However, when and why we can efficiently optimize on the sphere using simple first-order methods is poorly understood. We introduce Riemannian Gradient Alignment (RGA) as a unifying structural condition enabling fast convergence. RGA is a parameterized directional error bound requiring a tangent vector to sufficiently align with a target solution vector. We prove that Riemannian Gradient Descent with diminishing step sizes converges linearly when RGA holds with order $r=1$, and at rate $O(k^{-1/(2r-2)})$ for $r>1$. The result applies even to tangent vector fields that are not gradients of any objective. Our main technical contribution is a family of derivative-based sufficient conditions for RGA. We prove these conditions for a range of learning problems, including multi-instance learning/max pooling, Gaussian halfspaces, single-index and generalized linear models, phase retrieval, complete orthogonal dictionary learning, and (sparse) PCA. The provided examples span distributional families that include standard Gaussian, conditionally Gaussian, and more general structured distributions. The provided guarantees cover objectives that are generally not (geodesically) convex, may be nonsmooth, and may arise from discrete distributions. These results establish tractability of problem classes where no prior error bound conditions were known, as well as unify, strengthen, and generalize several prior results.

title: Dense Structural Compression of Transformers via Gauge-Correct Channel Removal
abstract: Inference energy per token drives the cost and carbon footprint of deployed transformers. It is dominated by dense matrix products that incur fused multiply-accumulate (FMA) operations and memory traffic. To reduce these computations while retaining dense tensors for high GPU throughput, we develop a methodology from first principles to adapt structural complexity during training to maximize inference utility per unit compute. Channel penalties drive entire tensor slices to zero to enable physical removal while preserving density and the network function. The natural approach, penalizing the norm of operator components acting through each channel, is provably destabilized by gauge freedom. We resolve this pathology with GaugeLasso: additive symmetric group-lasso penalties that recover a monotone function of product-norms when the network converges to gauge balance. Our equilibrium analysis enables per-channel calibration to correctly suppress slices that under-perform in inference utility per unit compute. Under adaptive pressure, the network reorganizes into depth-dependent structural profiles that can be far smaller than the architecture required to learn the task. On polynomial long division over $\mathbb{F}_{31}$, compute compresses from 148 to 255 times with perfect accuracy. On character-level language modeling, compressed models outperform the hand-designed baseline at equal FMA. On masked autoencoding, a compression trial exposes which axes were over-provisioned and which saturated, guiding a better second design. Compaction also accelerates training monotonically as the model progresses. Post-hoc pruning with the same utility ranking cannot reach these structures, showing that sustained pressure is central to discovery of efficient models. Retraining a discovered architecture recovers baseline quality on our statistical tasks, but fails on our exact algorithmic task.

title: CGSM: Concept-Guided Segmentation Model for Precise Pulmonary Lesion Delineation
abstract: Accurate segmentation of pulmonary lesions is essential for effective clinical diagnosis and treatment strategies. Existing segmentation approaches often lack task-specific semantic guidance, as text-based annotations typically offer coarse localization of lesions, leading to inadequate delineation of lesion boundaries and poor performance on small-scale lesions. To address this, we propose CGSM, a Concept-Guided Segmentation Model that integrates LLM-generated and clinically reviewed concepts into the segmentation process. Specifically, we design a Concept-Visual Alignment Module (CVAM) to activate relevant tokens within the concepts that align with visual features, enhancing the interaction between textual and visual information. In addition, we introduce a Concept Modulated Decoder (CM-Decoder), which uses concepts from CVAM as modulation signals to facilitate the adaptive fusion of image and text features, improving the segmentation accuracy. Extensive experiments on two public datasets show that CGSM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with results of 91.59% Dice and 84.49% mIoU on the QaTa-COV19 dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in pulmonary lesion segmentation.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QCES) – Faster Solution for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of Quantum Annealing (QA) to accelerate the solution of complex optimization problems, particularly those encountered in areas like logistics, resource allocation, and chemical synthesis. We propose a novel approach, Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Satisfaction (QCES), which leverages the strengths of QA to efficiently solve optimization problems by integrating it with traditional constraint satisfaction techniques. The core mechanism involves a hybrid algorithm that combines the advantages of both quantum annealing and constraint satisfaction, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational time compared to conventional methods. The paper details the architecture of the QCES system, explores its performance through simulations, and discusses potential future research directions.

title: Probability Topological Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neural network optimization algorithm based on probability topology, aiming to enhance the adaptability of neural networks to complex and noisy data. The core concept centers on representing the network's topology as a probability distribution, which serves as a guiding principle for the optimization process. This approach contrasts with traditional methods that primarily rely on gradient descent, offering a unique perspective on network design and training. We propose a framework where the network's topology is explicitly modeled and optimized, leading to improved generalization and robustness. The paper details the mathematical formulation of this algorithm, its key components, and demonstrates its effectiveness through experimental results on a dataset showcasing complex data patterns. We highlight the advantages of incorporating topology as a key optimization objective, ultimately contributing to a more robust and adaptable neural network architecture.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement measurement algorithm based on adaptive topology. The core objective is to enhance the accuracy of quantum entanglement measurement by leveraging the unique properties of topological structures. We propose a method that dynamically adjusts measurement parameters to achieve a significantly improved precision in quantifying the entanglement strength. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through rigorous analysis and simulations, highlighting its potential to significantly boost quantum information processing efficiency. This work addresses a critical challenge in quantum information science: achieving robust and accurate entanglement measurement.
